claims.source: Along the parallel axonal fibers of Kenyon cells (KCs), DANs and MB output neurons (MBONs) form 16 matched compartments (Aso et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020; Tanaka et al., 2008), which serve as units of associative learning.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: Reward and punishment activate distinct subsets of 20 types of DANs.
claims.source: Reward and punishment activate distinct subsets of 20 types of DANs (Berry et al., 2015; Burke et al., 2012; Kirkhart and Scott, 2015; Lewis et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2012; Riemensperger et al., 2005; Siju et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Individual DANs write and update memories in each compartment with cell-type-specific dynamics by modulating synaptic connection between KCs and MBONs.
claims.source: Individual DANs write and update memories in each compartment with cell-type-specific dynamics by modulating synaptic connection between KCs and MBONs (Aso et al., 2019; Aso et al., 2012; Aso and Rubin, 2016; Hige et al., 2015; Huetteroth et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015; Perisse et al., 2016; Vrontou et al., 2021; Yamagata et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies on synaptic plasticity.

claims.claim: MBON axons project to regions where DAN dendrites arborize, providing an anatomical pathway for feedback of memory-based information onto DANs.
claims.source: Outside the MB, MBON axons project to regions where DAN dendrites arborize; this provides an anatomical pathway for feedback of memory-based information onto DANs, a potential substrate for higher-order conditioning.
claims.evidence: This is based on anatomical observations and represents an inference about potential function.

claims.claim: DANs in the MB dynamically change odor responses after olfactory conditioning.
claims.source: Indeed, early studies showed that DANs in the MB dynamically change odor responses after olfactory conditioning (Riemensperger et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Large fractions of synaptic inputs to the MB's DANs originate from the MB itself in both larval and adult Drosophila.
claims.source: In both larval and adult Drosophila, large fractions of synaptic inputs to the MB's DANs originate from the MB itself (Eschbach et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to connectome studies.

claims.claim: Flies increased their preference to the S2+ odor over the S2− odor after five training sessions when first-order conditioning was long enough (5 min).
claims.source: After five training sessions, flies increased their preference to the S2+ odor over the S2− odor when first-order conditioning was long enough (i.e. 5 min; Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The preference for the S2+ odor was not due to sensory preconditioning.
claims.source: This preference for the S2+ odor was not due to sensory preconditioning, another form of higher-order conditioning in which S2-S1 pairing was done before pairing S1-sugar (Figure 1E)
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the control experiment shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Second-order memory after odor-sugar conditioning did not last for one day.
claims.source: Second-order memory after odor-sugar conditioning did not last for one day and was susceptible to extinction (Figure 1F and G).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 1F and G.

claims.claim: With optogenetic stimulation of sugar sensory neurons, the first-order memory steadily increased during nine training sessions, whereas second-order memory peaked at the third training and declined subsequently.
claims.source: With optogenetic stimulation of sugar sensory neurons, the first-order memory steadily increased during nine training sessions, whereas second-order memory peaked at the third training and declined subsequently (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: The transiency of learning was not observed when activation of sugar sensory neurons was not omitted during second-order conditioning.
claims.source: This transiency of learning was not observed when activation of sugar sensory neurons was not omitted during second-order conditioning (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the control experiment shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: Learning of association between S2+ odor and activation of sugar sensory neurons was compromised when S2+ is preceded by S1 which predicts the occurrence of reward.
claims.source: Learning of association between S2+ odor and activation of sugar sensory neurons was compromised when S2+ is preceded by S1 which predicts the occurrence of reward (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claims.claim: The transient and unstable nature of second-order memory observed across animal phyla also applies to Drosophila.
claims.source: These results indicate that the transient and unstable nature of second-order memory observed across animal phyla also applies to Drosophila, and the temporal order of the stimuli is crucial for second-order conditioning as in first-order conditioning.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and comparison with literature.

claims.claim: Among four sets of DAN cell types that can induce first-order appetitive memory, two sets — PAM-α1 and a combination of PAM-γ5 and β′2a — could induce significant second-order memory compared to the genetic control.
claims.source: Among four sets of DAN cell types that can induce first-order appetitive memory (Figure 2A), two sets — PAM-α1 and a combination of PAM-γ5 and β′2a — could induce significant second-order memory compared to the genetic control (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claims.claim: During second-order training following optogenetic first-order conditioning, S2 odor must precede the S1 odor.
claims.source: Furthermore, during second-order training following optogenetic first-order conditioning, S2 odor must precede the S1 odor (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Memory in PAM-α1 but not PAM-γ5/β′2a could instruct second-order conditioning one day after the first-order conditioning.
claims.source: As expected from those different stabilities of the first-order memory, memory in PAM-α1 but not PAM-γ5/β′2a could instruct second-order conditioning one day after the first-order conditioning (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Blocking of synaptic transmission from PAM-α1 DANs with Tetanus Toxin light chain abolished both S1 preference and second-order memory when assayed one day after odor-sugar conditioning.
claims.source: Consistent with the outcome of this optogenetic experiment, blocking of synaptic transmission from PAM-α1 DANs with Tetanus Toxin (TNT) light chain abolished both S1 preference and second-order memory when assayed one day after odor-sugar conditioning (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Blocking PAM cluster DANs in the γ4, γ5, β′2a with TNT impaired the second-order conditioning without affecting S1 preference.
claims.source: In contrast, blocking PAM cluster DANs in the γ4, γ5, β′2a with TNT impaired the second-order conditioning without affecting S1 preference (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The second-order memory derived from the first-order memory in the α1 compartment exhibited the transient learning curve.
claims.source: The second-order memory derived from the first-order memory in the α1 compartment exhibited the transient learning curve (Figure 2E–F) and susceptibility to extinction, recapitulating observations after odor-sugar conditioning (Figure 1F–H).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 2E-F.

claims.claim: α1 is the primary candidate compartment to store the first-order memory that instructs second-order conditioning.
claims.source: Thus, these results suggest α1 as the primary candidate compartment to store the first-order memory that instructs second-order conditioning.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results presented.

claims.claim: Pairing an odor and DAN activation leads to reduced spiking responses to that odor in MBON-α1.
claims.source: In MBON-α1, we found that pairing an odor and DAN activation leads to reduced spiking responses to that odor as in other MB compartments examined in previous studies (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Berry et al., 2018; Handler et al., 2019; Hige et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015; Owald and Waddell, 2015; Séjourné et al., 2011; Vrontou et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and supported by citations.

claims.claim: After a single round of second-order conditioning, MBON-γ5β′2a showed reduced responses to the S2+ odor, while responses to S2− did not change even after five repetitions of conditioning.
claims.source: After a single round of second-order conditioning, MBON-γ5β′2a showed reduced responses to the S2+ odor, while responses to S2− did not change even after five repetitions of conditioning (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 3B and C.

claims.claim: Repeated presentation of S2 odors without S1 did not cause a reduction of odor responses in MBON-γ5β′2a.
claims.source: Repeated presentation of S2 odors without S1 did not cause a reduction of odor responses (Figure 3D and E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the control experiment shown in Figures 3D and E.

claims.claim: The α1 compartment can instruct second-order conditioning in the γ5/β′2a and potentially other compartments.
claims.source: These results indicate that the α1 compartment can instruct second-order conditioning in the γ5/β′2a and potentially other compartments.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological results presented.

claims.claim: MBON-α1 is the sole output pathway from the α1 compartment.
claims.source: MBON-α1 is the sole output pathway from the α1 compartment and is, like other reward memory compartment MBONs, glutamatergic.
claims.evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge of the mushroom body circuit.

claims.claim: MBON-α1 is the only MBON that does not send direct output to DANs innervating other compartments.
claims.source: However, α1 appears to be an exceptionally isolated compartment. MBON-α1 is the only MBON that does not send direct output to DANs innervating other compartments; rather it only directly connects with the DANs that innervate the same compartment, PAM-α1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Li et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on connectome data cited from Li et al., 2020 and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: MBON-α1 shows very limited connections to DANs innervating other compartments that are mediated by a single interneuron (one-hop pathways).
claims.source: Similarly, MBON-α1 shows very limited connections to DANs innervating other compartments that are mediated by a single interneuron (one-hop pathways; Li et al., 2020; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is based on connectome data cited from Li et al., 2020 and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Prominent cholinergic two-hop pathways from MBON-α1 to multiple reward-DANs including PAM-γ5, γ4, β′2a, β′2m, β′2p are mediated by the interneurons SMP353/354 and SMP108.
claims.source: In this way (see Materials and methods for detail), we identified prominent cholinergic two-hop pathways from MBON-α1 to multiple reward-DANs including PAM-γ5, γ4, β′2a, β′2m, β′2p that were mediated by the interneurons SMP353/354 and SMP108 (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on connectome analysis and neurotransmitter prediction shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: SMP353/354 are a subset of the UpWind Neurons (UpWiNs) that transform appetitive memory into directional turning to the upwind orientation.
claims.source: The SMP353/354 are a subset of the UpWind Neurons (UpWiNs) that transform appetitive memory into directional turning to the upwind orientation (Aso et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Among all cholinergic neurons, SMP108 has the highest number of connections with reward DANs.
claims.source: Among all cholinergic neurons, SMP108 has the highest number of connections with reward DANs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on connectome analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: SMP108 synapses onto all three cholinergic interneurons (SMP177, LHPV5e1, LHPV10d1) in the second layer of the two-hop pathways, providing additional excitatory drive to PAM DANs.
claims.source: SMP108 also synapses onto all three cholinergic interneurons (SMP177, LHPV5e1, LHPV10d1) in the second layer of the two-hop pathways, providing additional excitatory drive to PAM DANs (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is based on connectome analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: SMP108 appeared as an outstanding cell type to receive direct inputs from MBON-γ5β′2a and output to DANs.
claims.source: Intriguingly, SMP108 also appeared as an outstanding cell type to receive direct inputs from MBON-γ5β′2a and output to DANs (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is based on connectome analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Axonal terminals of SMP108 are immunoreactive to choline acetyltransferase.
claims.source: Using these drivers, we confirmed that axonal terminals of SMP108 are immunoreactive to choline acetyltransferase (Figure 4E), which is consistent with the fact that 2416 out of 2753 presynaptic sites of SMP108 are predicted to be cholinergic in the hemibrain data (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4E and supported by connectome data.

claims.claim: After pairing an odor with optogenetic activation of PAM-cluster DANs, responses of SMP108 to the paired odor were selectively potentiated.
claims.source: After pairing, responses to the paired odor were selectively potentiated (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Reversal pairing de-potentiated the previously paired odor in SMP108.
claims.source: Furthermore, reversal pairing de-potentiated the previously paired odor.
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: SMP108 is capable of acquiring enhanced responses to S1 after first-order conditioning and flexibly tracking updates of odor-reward associations.
claims.source: Thus, SMP108 is capable of acquiring enhanced responses to S1 after first-order conditioning and flexibly tracking updates of odor-reward associations.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological results presented in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Activation of SMP108 or SMP353/354 evoked dopamine release in the reward memory compartments β′2, γ4 and γ5 compartments.
claims.source: Consistent with EM connectivity, activation of SMP108 or SMP353/354 evoked dopamine release in the reward memory compartments β′2, γ4 and γ5 compartments (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by dopamine imaging experiments shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: SMP108 activation also evoked small dopamine release in β1 and β2, presumably via indirect connections, but not in α1.
claims.source: SMP108 activation also evoked small dopamine release in β1 and β2, presumably via indirect connections, but not in α1.
claims.evidence: This is based on dopamine imaging data and represents an inference about the mechanism.

claims.claim: The dopamine signal in γ2, which is tuned to punitive stimuli, was significantly reduced after SMP108 activation.
claims.source: Notably, we observed that the dopamine signal in γ2, which is tuned to punitive stimuli, was significantly reduced after SMP108 activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by dopamine imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Activation of SMP108 triggers dopamine release selectively in multiple reward memory compartments.
claims.source: Thus, activation of SMP108 triggers dopamine release selectively in multiple reward memory compartments.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the dopamine imaging results presented.

claims.claim: Blocking neurotransmission of SMP108 by expression of TNT using two different split-GAL4 drivers impaired second-order conditioning compared to genetic controls.
claims.source: As expected from above results, we found that blocking neurotransmission of SMP108 by expression of TNT using two different split-GAL4 drivers impaired second-order conditioning compared to genetic controls (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Blocking SMP108 with TNT did not impair the first-order memory with 2 min or 1 day retention.
claims.source: Nonetheless, blocking SMP108 with TNT did not impair the first-order memory with 2 min or 1 day retention (Figure 7B), indicating that flies with blocked SMP108 were fully capable of smelling odors, tasting sugar, and forming, consolidating, and retrieving the first-order appetitive memory.
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Upon optogenetic stimulation of SMP108 with CsChrimson, flies changed their mean orientation and walked upwind in the circular arena.
claims.source: Upon optogenetic stimulation of SMP108 with CsChrimson, flies indeed changed their mean orientation and walked upwind in the same circular arena used in the olfactory conditioning experiments described above (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Upwind steering in response to the sugar-associated odor was not impaired in SMP108-blocked flies.
claims.source: However, we did not observe any impairment of upwind steering in response to the sugar-associated odor in SMP108-blocked flies (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), suggesting the existence of redundant circuits that trigger memory-based upwind steering.
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and represents an inference about circuit redundancy.

claims.claim: SMP108 could contribute to retrieval of reward memory for guiding actions, but its requirement is limited to second-order conditioning.
claims.source: Thus, SMP108 could contribute to retrieval of reward memory for guiding actions, but its requirement is limited to second-order conditioning.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral results presented.

claims.claim: SMP108 plays a key role in second-order conditioning by triggering dopamine signals in response to the reward-predicting cue.
claims.source: These hierarchical connections between dopamine subsystems explain distinct properties of first- and second-order memory long known by behavioral psychologists.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined results of connectome analysis, functional experiments, and behavioral assays.

claims.claim: Memories induced by SMP108 or its upstream SMP353/354 differ in several ways from the memory induced by activation of PAM-α1.
claims.source: These experiments revealed that memories induced by SMP108 or its upstream SMP353/354 differ in several ways from the memory induced by activation of PAM-α1 (Figure 8C–F).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figures 8C-F.

claims.claim: SMP108 and SMP353/354 can induce memory more rapidly than PAM-α1.
claims.source: First, SMP108 and SMP353/354 can induce memory more rapidly than PAM-α1 (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Memories formed by SMP108 and SMP353/354 declined during later training sessions and during the extinction phase, whereas memory formed by PAM-α1 remained high.
claims.source: Second, memories formed by SMP108 and SMP353/354 declined during later training sessions and during the extinction phase, whereas memory formed by PAM-α1 remained high (Figure 8D and E).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figures 8D and E.

claims.claim: Memory formed by PAM-α1 was resistant to DAN activation, but memories formed by SMP108 and SMP353/354 were decreased.
claims.source: Third, memory formed by PAM-α1 was resistant to DAN activation, but memories formed by SMP108 and SMP353/354 were decreased (Figure 8F).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 8F.

claims.claim: Transient learning and fast extinction observed with SMP108 and SMP353/354 activation are reminiscent of second-order conditioning by sugar or optogenetics.
claims.source: Such transient learning and fast extinction are reminiscent of second-order conditioning by sugar (Figure 1F and G) or optogenetics (Figures 1H, 2E and G).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of experimental results.

claims.claim: Drivers that target CsChrimson to SMP108's downstream DANs exhibited memory dynamics similar to those observed when CsChrimson is activated in SMP108 or SMP353/354.
claims.source: In contrast to the activation of CsChrimson in PAM-α1, drivers that target CsChrimson to SMP108's downstream DANs exhibited memory dynamics similar to those observed when CsChrimson is activated in SMP108 or SMP353/354.
claims.evidence: This is based on behavioral experiments shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: MB032B and MB213B split-GAL4 that target CsChrimson in β′2m and β1/β2, respectively, induced transient memories.
claims.source: For instance, MB032B and MB213B split-GAL4 that target CsChrimson in β′2m and β1/β2, respectively, induced transient memories (Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: This is directly demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: Fitting the memory dynamics formed by SMP108 with a linear sum of direct DAN activation data indicated an overweight of MB032B (β′2m), MB213B (β1/β2) and MB312C (γ4), and zero weight for MB043C (α1).
claims.source: Consistent with this, fitting the memory dynamics formed by SMP108 with a linear sum of direct DAN activation data indicated an overweight of MB032B (β′2m), MB213B (β1/β2) and MB312C (γ4), and zero weight for MB043C (α1) (Figure 8G).
claims.evidence: This is based on computational analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 8G.

claims.claim: The high memory score of SMP108 activation after the first 10 s training was fitted poorly, indicating that combinatorial activation of DANs and/or suppression of DANs innervating γ2 might have a synergistic effect on memory formation.
claims.source: However, the high memory score of SMP108 activation after the first 10 s training was fitted poorly, indicating that combinatorial activation of DANs and/or suppression of DANs innervating γ2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) might have a synergistic effect on memory formation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results and dopamine imaging data.

claims.claim: The distinct memory properties exhibited by upstream and downstream partners of SMP108 might help explain the circuit mechanisms underlying the difference between first- and second-order memories.
claims.source: These experiments highlight the distinct memory properties exhibited by upstream and downstream partners of SMP108, and might help explain the circuit mechanisms underlying the difference between first- and second-order memories.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Formation of second-order memory was most effective either when the first-order S1 odor predicted a strong sugar reward or when long-term first-order memory was optogenetically induced.
claims.source: Our optimization of the second-order conditioning protocol using actual sugar reward or its optogenetic substitution revealed important properties of second-order memory and enabled detailed circuit interrogation. Formation of second-order memory was most effective either when the first-order S1 odor predicted a strong sugar reward (Figure 1D) or when long-term first-order memory was optogenetically induced (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental results shown in Figures 1D and 2B.

claims.claim: Requirement of long first-order training for successful formation of second-order memory can be explained by the properties of the α1 compartment.
claims.source: Requirement of long first-order training for successful formation of second-order memory (Figure 1C and D) can be explained by the properties of the α1, which we identified as the teacher compartment.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and the properties of the α1 compartment.

claims.claim: The DANs in α1 respond to sugar relatively weakly compared to other DANs in the β′2, β2, γ4, γ5 compartments.
claims.source: The DANs in α1 respond to sugar relatively weakly compared to other DANs in the β′2, β2, γ4, γ5 compartments (Siju et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The α1 compartment exhibited the slowest learning rate of all compartments even with optogenetic stimulation of DANs that efficiently release dopamine.
claims.source: Also the α1 compartment exhibited the slowest learning rate of all compartments even with optogenetic stimulation of DANs that efficiently release dopamine (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Once established, memory in the α1 is highly resistant to extinction.
claims.source: Once established, however, memory in the α1 is highly resistant to extinction (Figures 2A and 8D), which is likely critical for forming second-order conditioning without compromising first-order memory.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 8D.

claims.claim: The eligibility of the α1 compartment as a teaching compartment is emphasized by its slow learning rate and resistance to extinction.
claims.source: These considerations emphasize the eligibility of the α1 compartment as a teaching compartment among all reward-memory compartments.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and properties of the α1 compartment.

claims.claim: Transient and unstable nature of second-order memory can be ascribed to collective properties of student compartments.
claims.source: On the other hand, transient and unstable nature of second-order memory can be ascribed to collective properties of student compartments (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Heterogeneous populations of DANs are found in vertebrate species, and they are involved in distinct types of learning.
claims.source: Importantly, heterogeneous populations of DANs are also found in vertebrate species, and they are involved in distinct types of learning.
claims.evidence: This is based on general knowledge of dopaminergic systems in vertebrates.

claims.claim: Studies using visual conditioning in monkeys found that distinct types of DANs projecting to the head or tail regions of the caudate nucleus change their response to reward-predicting cues with very different dynamics.
claims.source: Studies using visual conditioning in monkeys found that distinct types of DANs projecting to the head or tail regions of the caudate nucleus change their response to reward-predicting cues with very different dynamics (Kim et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in monkeys.

claims.claim: A recent study in rodents indicated that subsets of DANs have diverse learning rates to compute positive and negative reward prediction errors to enable distributional reinforcement learning.
claims.source: A recent study in rodents indicated that subsets of DANs have diverse learning rates to compute positive and negative reward prediction errors to enable distributional reinforcement learning (Dabney et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study in rodents.

claims.claim: Cue-evoked dopamine transients could be derived from memory encoded by the same DAN, other type(s) of DANs, or both, depending on the architecture of feedback circuits.
claims.source: Such dopamine transients could be derived from memory encoded by the same DAN, other type(s) of DANs, or both, depending on the architecture of feedback circuits.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms.

claims.claim: Future studies in vertebrate models may reveal a hierarchical interaction between dopamine cell types with fast and slow dynamics in second-order conditioning.
claims.source: Given the conserved nature of second-order memory transiency across animal phyla, future studies in vertebrate models may also reveal a hierarchical interaction between dopamine cell types with fast and slow dynamics in second-order conditioning.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claims.claim: In flies, feedback and feedforward connections between MBONs and DANs or lateral connections between MBONs are implicated in extinction of aversive and appetitive memory as well as consolidation of memories.
claims.source: In fact, in flies, feedback and feedforward connections between MBONs and DANs or lateral connections between MBONs are implicated in extinction of aversive and appetitive memory as well as consolidation of memories (Felsenberg et al., 2018; Felsenberg et al., 2017; McCurdy et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The EM connectome map, along with computational modeling, will guide further investigation of intercompartmental interactions.
claims.source: The EM connectome map, along with computational modeling (Gkanias et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2021), will guide further investigation of intercompartmental interactions.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about future research directions supported by citations.

claims.claim: LHCENT3 may serve as the substrate for subtraction of expected reward in the computation of reward prediction error, as GABAergic neurons in VTA do in vertebrate brains.
claims.source: For instance, we identified one outlier cell type of GABAergic interneuron LHCENT3 that receives inputs from glutamatergic MBON-γ5β′2a and outputs to reward DANs (Figure 4C). This cell type may serve as the substrate for subtraction of expected reward in the computation of reward prediction error, as GABAergic neurons in VTA do in vertebrate brains (Starkweather and Uchida, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on connectome data and comparison with vertebrate systems.

claims.claim: It is unlikely that flies associate S2 with a specific type of reward used as US, because individual MB compartments are tuned to different kinds of rewards or reward responses.
claims.source: Our finding of the cross-compartmental nature of second-order conditioning makes it unlikely that flies associate S2 with a specific type of reward used as US, because individual MB compartments are tuned to different kinds of rewards or reward responses.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and known properties of MB compartments.

claims.claim: DANs in the teacher compartment α1 are essential for nutritional value learning.
claims.source: That is, while DANs in the teacher compartment α1 are essential for nutritional value learning (Yamagata et al., 2015), those in the student compartments γ4 and β′2 respond to water in thirsty flies (Lin et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: DANs in the student compartments γ4 and β′2 respond to water in thirsty flies.
claims.source: those in the student compartments γ4 and β′2 respond to water in thirsty flies (Lin et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: DANs in γ4, γ5 and β′2 also represent vinegar and activity of DANs in γ4 correlates with upwind steering.
claims.source: DANs in γ4, γ5 and β′2 also represent vinegar and activity of DANs in γ4 correlates with upwind steering (Lewis et al., 2015; Zolin et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: DANs in β′2a also respond to a punishment-predicting odor when punishment is omitted.
claims.source: DANs in β′2a also respond to a punishment-predicting odor when punishment is omitted (McCurdy et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: S2 is associated with positive valence that was originally associated with S1 but generalized to broader types of rewards.

results.result: Drosophila exhibits second-order conditioning with distinct temporal dynamics: flies learn to prefer S2+ over S2- after five training sessions when first-order conditioning is sufficiently long (5 min), but this memory is transient, decays within one day, is susceptible to extinction, and requires proper temporal ordering of stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C26 collectively demonstrate robust second-order conditioning in Drosophila with experimental controls. The data show preference for S2+ (C20), rule out sensory preconditioning (C21), demonstrate memory decay (C22), show transient learning curves (C23-C24), confirm temporal order requirements (C25), and establish conservation with other species (C26). Multiple experimental paradigms and controls support these findings.

results.result: The α1 compartment serves as the primary 'teacher' compartment for second-order conditioning: PAM-α1 DANs can induce second-order memory one day after first-order conditioning, blocking PAM-α1 abolishes both first-order and second-order memory, while blocking other compartments selectively impairs second-order conditioning without affecting first-order memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C33 provide converging evidence from optogenetic activation (C27-C29), genetic silencing (C30-C31), and temporal dynamics (C32) that identify α1 as the teacher compartment. The dissociation between effects on first-order versus second-order memory (C30-C31) is particularly compelling. Multiple driver lines and experimental approaches support this conclusion.

results.result: First-order memory in the α1 compartment induces secondary plasticity in the γ5/β'2a compartment: pairing odor with PAM-α1 activation reduces MBON-α1 responses, and subsequent second-order conditioning selectively reduces MBON-γ5β'2a responses to S2+ but not S2-.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 demonstrate cross-compartmental plasticity using electrophysiology. The selective depression of S2+ responses in MBON-γ5β'2a after second-order conditioning (C35), with appropriate controls (C36), provides direct evidence for the teacher-student model. The inference (C37) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Connectome analysis identifies SMP108 as a key cholinergic interneuron mediating hierarchical connections from α1 to other reward compartments: MBON-α1 connects to multiple reward DANs via two-hop pathways through SMP353/354 and SMP108, with SMP108 having the highest number of connections to reward DANs among cholinergic neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C46 are based on systematic connectome analysis (C39-C41, C43-C45) and validated by immunohistochemistry (C46). The identification of SMP108 as an outstanding hub is supported by quantitative connectivity data. The neurotransmitter prediction and experimental validation strengthen these anatomical findings.

results.result: SMP108 acquires enhanced responses to reward-predicting odors after first-order conditioning and flexibly tracks odor-reward associations: responses to paired odors are selectively potentiated, and reversal pairing de-potentiates previously paired odors.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 are directly supported by electrophysiological recordings showing selective potentiation (C47) and reversibility (C48). The data demonstrate that SMP108 can acquire and update odor-reward associations, supporting its proposed role in second-order conditioning.

results.result: Activation of SMP108 triggers dopamine release selectively in multiple reward memory compartments: SMP108 activation evokes dopamine release in β'2, γ4, and γ5 compartments, with smaller release in β1 and β2, but not in α1, and reduces dopamine in the punishment-tuned γ2 compartment.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 are supported by dopamine imaging experiments using DA2m sensor. The pattern of dopamine release is consistent with EM connectivity predictions. The selective activation of reward compartments and suppression of punishment compartments (C52) provides functional validation of the circuit architecture.

results.result: SMP108 is required for second-order conditioning but not first-order memory: blocking SMP108 with TNT impairs second-order conditioning while leaving first-order memory intact, and SMP108 activation can trigger upwind steering but is not required for memory-based upwind steering.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C59 demonstrate the specific requirement of SMP108 for second-order conditioning using genetic silencing (C54-C55) and behavioral assays (C56-C57). The dissociation between second-order conditioning and first-order memory (C55) is critical. The redundancy in upwind steering circuits (C57) is appropriately noted.

results.result: Memories induced by SMP108 and SMP353/354 exhibit transient dynamics distinct from PAM-α1: they form more rapidly, decline during training and extinction, and are susceptible to DAN activation, recapitulating second-order memory properties. Linear modeling suggests SMP108 activates multiple downstream compartments with transient dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C69 provide comprehensive characterization of memory dynamics using optogenetics and behavioral assays. The comparison between SMP108/SMP353/354 and PAM-α1 (C61-C63) demonstrates distinct properties. The linear modeling (C67) provides quantitative support, though the poor fit for early training (C68) suggests additional complexity. The overall pattern strongly supports the teacher-student model.

results.result: The distinct properties of teacher (α1) and student compartments explain second-order memory dynamics: α1 has slow learning rate, weak sugar responses, and high resistance to extinction, making it suitable as a teacher, while student compartments have fast, transient dynamics that account for second-order memory transiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C76 synthesize experimental findings to explain behavioral observations. The characterization of α1 properties (C72-C74) is supported by cited data and current experiments. The inference about teacher-student roles (C75-C76) is well-supported by the collective evidence, though some properties rely on cited work.

results.result: Second-order conditioning in Drosophila involves association with generalized positive valence rather than specific reward features: the cross-compartmental nature of second-order conditioning and differential tuning of compartments to various rewards suggest S2 is associated with broad positive valence, consistent with behavioral observations across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C94 provide a mechanistic interpretation of second-order conditioning content. The inference (C85, C90) is well-supported by the circuit architecture and known compartment functions (C86-C89). The consistency with behavioral literature (C91-C93) strengthens the interpretation. This provides a concrete circuit-level explanation for psychological phenomena.

results.result: The Drosophila mushroom body comprises anatomically and functionally distinct dopaminergic compartments with cell-type-specific memory dynamics and interconnections that provide substrates for higher-order learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C14-C19 establish the anatomical and functional organization of the MB circuit based on extensive prior literature. These are well-established facts supported by multiple citations. The claims provide essential background for understanding the current work.

results.result: Second-order conditioning is a conserved form of higher-order learning across animal phyla with characteristic properties including transiency, susceptibility to extinction, and association with general valence rather than specific reinforcer features.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C13 summarize established behavioral literature on second-order conditioning. All claims are supported by appropriate citations. These provide important context for the current study but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: SMP353/354 are a subset of UpWind Neurons that transform appetitive memory into directional turning.
results.evaluation: Claim C42 is supported by citation to a previous study. This provides context for understanding SMP353/354 function but is not a new finding of this manuscript.

results.result: Heterogeneous dopamine neuron populations with distinct learning dynamics are found in vertebrate species and contribute to various forms of learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 summarize relevant vertebrate literature. These are well-supported by citations and provide important comparative context, but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: A slow and stable memory compartment (α1) serves as a 'teacher' by instructing faster, transient memory compartments via the excitatory interneuron SMP108, which acquires enhanced responses to reward-predicting odors and evokes dopamine release in student compartments, explaining distinct properties of first- and second-order memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C6 represent the main conclusions of the manuscript, synthesizing findings from multiple experimental approaches. These are well-supported by the detailed results (C20-C76) and provide a comprehensive mechanistic explanation for second-order conditioning. The hierarchical circuit architecture is validated through connectomics, physiology, and behavior.

results.result: Future studies may reveal hierarchical interactions between dopamine cell types in vertebrate second-order conditioning, and the EM connectome will guide investigation of intercompartmental interactions including potential reward prediction error computation by GABAergic interneurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81, C83-C84 are speculative statements about future research directions. While C84 identifies LHCENT3 based on connectome data, its proposed function is speculative. These represent reasonable hypotheses but lack experimental validation in the current work.

results.result: Feedback and feedforward connections between MBONs and DANs are implicated in memory extinction and consolidation in Drosophila.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 summarizes prior work on MBON-DAN interactions. This is well-supported by citations and provides relevant context, but represents prior knowledge.
